candidateRows: The existence of evil presupposes objective morality and natural teleology, both of which require God, so evil supports theism rather than atheism.
This is the first of Eric's three announced arguments and directly reverses a major atheistic argument by making evil evidence for God's existence.
After outlining his cumulative strategy, Eric argues that evil requires an objective moral standard and goal-directed proper functioning, neither of which he thinks atheism can supply.
Atheistic evolution supplies an undercutting defeater for trusting human cognition because natural selection favors adaptive behavior rather than true belief.
The argument is one of Eric's three principal pillars and claims that knowledge and rationality themselves make atheism self-defeating.
Eric defines knowledge, illustrates epistemic defeat with an unreliable clock, and argues that unguided evolution similarly defeats confidence in cognition and atheistic belief.
Consciousness and libertarian free will require an immaterial soul that naturalism excludes, so their existence counts against atheism and for theism.
This is the third principal argument in Eric's announced case and connects consciousness, agency, responsibility, and rational belief directly to theism.
Eric contends that mental properties cannot be reduced to physical properties and that physical causal closure would eliminate libertarian agency, responsibility, and intellectual integrity.
Naturalism begins with a theoretical advantage over theism because it posits fewer fundamental kinds of entities, causes, agents, and powers.
Qualitative simplicity supplies the comparative baseline for Justin's entire cumulative case and affects how all later evidence is weighed between the worldviews.
Justin defines naturalism as one basic kind of stuff governed by scientifically revealed laws and argues that theism adds ontological categories without an initial compensating benefit.
The long evolutionary history of severe suffering among nonmoral animals is more probable under indifferent naturalism than under perfectly good theism.
Animal suffering is the first of Justin's three principal evidential arguments and directly compares its expectedness under naturalism and theism.
Justin contrasts naturalism's expectation of fragile evolved organisms with a creator's freedom to make other forms of life, including systems without predation and prolonged animal misery.
The universe's near-total hostility to embodied moral agents is expected on naturalism but surprising if a rational, value-oriented God created the physical world.
Cosmic hostility is one of Justin's three announced principal facts and argues that the physical universe poorly reflects the highest known physically realizable value.
Justin argues that life-permitting regions should be rare under naturalism, whereas a value-oriented creator should make the physical world substantially more compatible with embodied moral life.
The existence and uneven distribution of nonresistant nonbelief are more expected if religious belief spreads naturally than if a perfectly loving God seeks relationship with everyone.
This is Justin's third principal evidential argument and directly tests perfect divine love against sincere unbelief and its geographic and historical distribution.

Justin reasons that perfect love would provide receptive people sufficient grounds for belief, yet sincere unbelief exists and varies across cultures and eras in ways natural diffusion readily explains.
Schieber's naturalism entails physicalism and determinism, leaving it unable to accommodate the immaterial realities on which his own case relies.
The move attacks the internal coherence of the opposing worldview and attempts to undercut all of its evidential arguments at once.
Schieber's definition of naturalism and his appeal to consciousness, evil, and other allegedly real features.
After challenging the weight assigned to simplicity, Hernandez argues that Schieber must reduce immaterial features to physical entities or eliminate them, with either option collapsing his case.

Animal suffering does not favor naturalism because naturalism cannot first explain consciousness, while theism can predict and explain suffering through free will, soul-building, the fall, and restoration.
This is the principal theistic response to evolutionary animal suffering, one of Schieber's three central arguments for naturalism.
Schieber's claim that extensive suffering among nonmoral sentient animals is substantially more expected on naturalism than on theism.
Hernandez first treats consciousness as a prerequisite that naturalism cannot explain, then supplies several theistic expectations and theodicies for animal suffering and its ultimate defeat.

The universe's apparent hostility to life does not support naturalism because life itself is unexpected without fine-tuning, cosmic emptiness contributes to habitability, and vastness can express divine artistry.
The passage directly contests Schieber's cosmic-hostility evidence and offers both scientific-purpose and divine-artistry explanations of the data.
Schieber's argument that a vast universe overwhelmingly hostile to moral sentient life is surprising on theism and expected on naturalism.

Hernandez rejects the assumption that God would make most of the universe habitable, invokes fine-tuning and the functional role of cosmic emptiness, and compares creation's vastness to artistic abundance.
Divine hiddenness does not disconfirm theism because perfect love need not entail constant openness, and God may hide to limit culpability, prevent aggravated apostasy, or prepare a later conversion.
This passage supplies the main theistic rebuttal to non-resistant nonbelief, one of the three pillars of Schieber's cumulative naturalistic case.
Schieber's contention that a perfectly loving God would always remain open to relationship with every non-resistant person.
Hernandez disputes the theological premise behind hiddenness, distinguishes belief from relationship, and argues that temporary or protective hiddenness can itself serve loving and merciful purposes.

Objective morality does not require God because irreducible normative truths can possess authority independently, while grounding obligation in divine commands or God's nature creates circularity and subjectivism.
The move directly answers Hernandez's first major argument for theism and offers non-theistic moral realism as a competing account of moral authority and objectivity.
Hernandez's argument that atheism cannot ground objective, universal, authoritative, and prescriptive moral values and duties.

Schieber denies that teleology is required for every metaethical system, challenges divine-command authority as circular, criticizes Hernandez's definition of objectivity, and recommends non-theistic moral realism.

Irreducible consciousness and meaningful freedom do not require souls, since naturalism can posit intrinsic phenomenal properties and can understand freedom compatibilistically as reasons-responsive action.
It answers two linked supports for Hernandez's immaterial-soul argument by presenting naturalistic alternatives for consciousness and agency.
Hernandez's claim that irreducible consciousness and libertarian free will establish an immaterial soul and thereby support God's existence.

Schieber grants that consciousness may resist physical reduction but proposes fundamental phenomenal properties rather than souls, then argues that reasons-responsive compatibilist freedom survives determinism.
Causal determination is compatible with rationality, as deterministic systems can reason, so the determination of a belief does not establish that the belief was irrationally acquired.
The response targets the inference connecting determinism to irrationality, which is essential to Hernandez's rationality-based case against atheism.
Hernandez's argument that a causally determined belief in atheism cannot have been rationally acquired or rationally affirmed.

Schieber uses deterministic computers as a counterexample to the claimed incompatibility, adding that whether computers are designed does not rescue the original inference about determination and rationality.

Naturalism and evolution need not defeat trust in cognition because adaptive success generally favors reliable belief-forming mechanisms and belief content can be causally connected to behavior and environmental fit.
This is the principal answer to Hernandez's knowledge argument, defending the epistemic viability of naturalism against a purported global defeater.
Hernandez's Plantinga-style claim that naturalism plus evolution supplies a global defeater for the reliability of every belief, including naturalism.

Schieber argues that broadly unreliable faculties lose adaptive value across varied situations, explains how belief content can guide behavior under naturalism, and turns a justification challenge back toward divine cognition.
Naturalism need not be strict physicalism: it may recognize abstract moral properties and fundamental phenomenal features while maintaining only one basic kind of concrete entity.
The clarification directly repairs the interpretation on which Hernandez's broad internal-incoherence objection depended and preserves Schieber's moral and consciousness commitments.
Hernandez's interpretation that Schieber's single-basic-stuff definition excludes moral properties, irreducible consciousness, and every nonphysical entity.

Schieber distinguishes concrete from abstract entities, affirms moral realism, and sketches a view on which physics describes relations while phenomenal properties belong at reality's fundamental level.
If consciousness exists at reality's fundamental level, Schieber has approached significant common ground with Christianity's claim that reality ultimately derives from mind.
The move attempts to convert Schieber's fundamental-consciousness view from a defense of naturalism into positive comparative support for mind-first theism.
Schieber's clarification that intrinsic phenomenal or proto-phenomenal properties may occur at the fundamental level of natural reality.
Hernandez explores Schieber's Russellian or panpsychist family of views and argues that their fundamental mentality resembles the Christian position that everything ultimately comes from God's mind.
Naturalism loses simplicity and explanatory power when it adds irreducible moral and conscious properties instead of reducing them to the physical.
The move directly challenges naturalism's advertised explanatory economy and argues that its accommodations of consciousness and morality weaken its comparative case.
Schieber's claim that consciousness may be an irreducible intrinsic aspect of fundamentally physical reality.
After Schieber describes science as silent about intrinsic nature, Hernandez argues that multiplying irreducible nonphysical features makes naturalism increasingly selective and costly.
Accepting irreducible consciousness is a motivated inference from consciousness and the limits of physics, rather than an ad hoc rescue of naturalism.
This reply protects naturalism from a major simplicity objection by explaining why its additional intrinsic properties are evidentially motivated despite their strangeness.
Hernandez's charge that irreducible conscious properties make naturalism ad hoc and reduce its simplicity and explanatory power.
Schieber concedes some loss of simplicity but argues that undeniable consciousness, its irreducibility, and physics' epistemic limits jointly motivate his monist account.
Grounding moral value in God's nature remains metaethical subjectivism because God is a person and therefore a subject.
The move contests a principal theistic argument by denying that divine grounding supplies the objective morality Hernandez claims theism uniquely explains.
Hernandez's opening claim that objective moral value is grounded in God as the ultimate moral standard.
When the discussion turns to evil and morality, Schieber argues that dependence on the nature of any person, including God, is dependence on a subject.
Objective morality is standardly understood as truth independent of human thought, so divine grounding is compatible with moral objectivity under a common definition.
This definitional defense is necessary for Hernandez's moral argument because it preserves the claim that God can ground morality without making it human-subjective.
Schieber's contention that Hernandez uses objective morality nonstandardly and that grounding value in a divine person is subjectivist.
Hernandez appeals to a secular moral philosopher's formulation and contrasts objective truths independent of human opinion with morality dependent on human judgment.
A deeper form of objectivity must be independent of every particular person, so morality grounded in God's nature cannot be ultimately objective.
The distinction prevents the definitional reply from resolving the dispute and sharpens the con case that divine moral grounding retains an arbitrary personal basis.
Hernandez's cited definition of objective morality as moral truth independent specifically of human thought and opinion.
Schieber grants that one usage may exclude only human opinion but argues that substantive ultimate objectivity cannot rely on any person's nature, including God's.
Necessary, eternal, personal moral properties are best grounded in a necessary, eternal, personal transcendent being rather than in finite subjects or abstractions.
This is the positive grounding inference at the heart of the pro moral argument, connecting the alleged features of morality to the attributes of God.
Schieber's objection that calling a God-grounded moral standard objective is arbitrary, ad hoc, and dependent on a subject.
Hernandez argues that morality's necessity, eternality, and personal or obligation-conferring character point toward a transcendent personal ground rather than a finite individual.
Evolutionary animal suffering is especially evidential because predatory body plans appear properly directed toward tearing apart and consuming other animals.
The move states a principal evidential argument from animal suffering against theism, focusing on apparently designed predatory functions rather than generic evil.
Hernandez's use of teleology and evil in support of theism and the moderator's request to examine his argument from suffering.
Returning to the argument from evil, Schieber emphasizes that many animals function normally precisely when their evolved anatomy inflicts severe suffering on prey.
Animal suffering can be attributed to humanity's fall, which affected all creation and deviated nature from its intended teleology, potentially even from the beginning.
This supplies the principal theistic explanation offered in the exchange for predation and animal suffering, directly addressing a major component of the con case.
Schieber's evolutionary argument that predatory animal structures and suffering appear teleologically normal and count against theism.
Hernandez says human disobedience affected animals, plants, and the wider creation, and suggests divine foreknowledge could permit fallen conditions throughout natural history.
The fall explanation lacks a specified mechanism and fine-grained predictive power connecting human sin to predatory anatomy and non-vegetarian ecosystems.
The objection attacks the explanatory adequacy of the pro theodicy by arguing that it accommodates observed suffering retrospectively without predicting its specific forms.
Hernandez's proposal that humanity's fall altered all creation and can explain animal predation even across earlier natural history.
Schieber asks what conditions would precede the fall and how sin could transform peaceful creatures into animals anatomically equipped to tear one another apart.
A successful theodicy must be more probable than its negation given theism and must jointly with theism explain the specific evil under dispute.
These criteria establish the evaluative burden for the fall defense and explain why merely predicting unspecified bad consequences does not answer the evidential argument.
Hernandez's broad claim that departing from God's plan predictably produces horrible consequences and thereby accounts for worldly suffering.
Schieber formalizes his challenge by requiring both antecedent plausibility and explanatory fit, then argues that Hernandez's fall account lacks enough substance for either assessment.
Cooperative inquiry does not justify divine hiddenness because shared exploration of God's nature can occur after everyone already believes God exists.
This directly defends the non-resistant nonbelief argument against a proposed relationship-building reason for God to leave his existence uncertain.
The proposal that divine hiddenness enables valuable human cooperation in bringing others to knowledge of God's love.
An audience member proposes that mediated discovery creates cooperative goods; Justin accepts those goods but argues that belief itself need not remain hidden for deeper joint inquiry.
Determinism is compatible with rational belief formation, as determined computers supply a counterexample to the alleged incompatibility between determination and rationality.
The move directly contests the free-thinking objection to naturalism and protects the rational coherence of belief formation under deterministic processes.
The claim that a belief produced within a deterministic causal order cannot have been formed through a genuinely rational process.
Justin identifies the challenged premise as an incompatibility between causation and rationality, then invokes deterministic computation to reject that general principle.
Naturalistic determination originates in non-rational causes, so it cannot secure rational thought merely by comparing minds to computers whose outputs depend on programmers.
This is the theistic counterreply on whether atheistic naturalism can explain trustworthy rationality, one of the debate's expressly identified explanatory domains.
Justin's computer analogy offered as a counterexample to the alleged incompatibility of deterministic causation and rational inference.
Eric distinguishes a programmed system's output from rational agency and argues that naturalism attempts to derive rationality from wholly non-rational determining conditions.
Evolutionary success does not require true beliefs because adaptive behavior depends on neurological structures, leaving naturalism unable to guarantee reliable metaphysical cognition.
The move develops the evolutionary argument against naturalism, challenging whether natural selection supplies a dependable route to truth rather than merely adaptive conduct.
Justin's earlier response to Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism, including his treatment of adaptive false beliefs.
Eric revisits the disputed illustration, argues that even a false self-conception could enhance reproductive behavior, and separates behavioral adaptation from belief truth.
Widespread contradictory metaphysical beliefs show that human metaphysical cognition is empirically unreliable, which creates a problem for theism rather than uniquely for naturalism.
This reverses the reliability objection by arguing that observed disagreement burdens a theistic account that places importance on correct metaphysical belief.
Eric's claim that evolutionary naturalism undermines confidence in the truth and reliability of human metaphysical belief formation.
Justin appeals to pervasive metaphysical disagreement as evidence of domain-specific unreliability and argues that such unreliability is especially difficult for theism to explain.
Consciousness is irreducible to ordinary physical causation and is plausibly a fundamental feature of reality that physics describes relationally without revealing intrinsically.
The move supplies Justin's naturalistic explanation of consciousness, directly addressing a principal explanatory category in the debate's motion without adopting reductive physicalism.
The challenge asking how consciousness can arise or be accommodated within Justin's naturalistic account of fundamental reality.
Justin distinguishes physics' mathematical and dispositional descriptions from intrinsic nature, treats consciousness as undeniable and irreducible, and places it at reality's base level.
If consciousness is fundamental, the best explanation of finite consciousness is an ultimate divine consciousness, while Justin's view lacks comparable simplicity and predictive power.
This presents the core theistic inference from fundamental consciousness to God and compares the rival views using explanatory simplicity, power, and predictability.
Justin's proposal that irreducible consciousness belongs at the fundamental level of reality without being identified with a divine mind.
Eric accepts that consciousness is basic but argues that a divine mind better predicts and explains finite minds than treating consciousness as an unexplained fundamental feature.
Plantinga's free-will defense has significant problems and does not exhaust logical arguments from evil, so the logical problem of evil remains viable despite its technical complexity.
The move directly contests the claim that the logical problem of evil has been resolved and preserves evil as evidence against the explanatory adequacy of theism.
Eric's claim that Plantinga's free-will defense solved the logical problem of evil and shifted the live debate to evidential formulations.
Justin rejects the standard historical narrative, notes objections to the free-will defense, and points to independent logical formulations that remain philosophically active.
Animal suffering is intrinsically bad even where animals lack moral responsibility, and a perfectly loving God therefore requires a plausible explanation for allowing such suffering.
This isolates morally unchosen animal suffering from culpable wrongdoing and states the evidential tension between creaturely suffering and a perfectly loving deity.
The request to explain whether animal suffering is evil and how Justin's worldview accounts for suffering without blaming non-rational creatures.
Justin distinguishes bad states of affairs from blameworthy agency, conditions responsibility on higher-order capacities, and argues that divine love makes permitted suffering demand explanation.
God may permit earthly suffering for free-will and afterlife-related goods, while theism also better grounds moral responsibility and the objective standard required to classify suffering as evil.
This combines a theistic justification for permitted suffering with objections to naturalistic responsibility and moral standards, directly answering the animal-suffering challenge.
Justin's argument that intrinsically bad creaturely suffering creates an unresolved evidential demand for any perfectly loving divine creator.
Eric invokes freedom, an afterlife, and the formative role of suffering, then returns to causal responsibility and divine grounding as parts of the theistic explanation.
Christian theism provides better predictions and explanations than naturalism, which faces particular difficulty accounting for consciousness and objective moral values.
This closing move directly states the pro side's comparative standard and applies it to central phenomena named in the debate motion.
Schieber's preceding case that naturalism compares favorably with theism across the debated phenomena.
In his closing, Hernandez summarizes the debate as an explanatory comparison and argues that Schieber has not established naturalism's superiority over theism.
Molinism is incompatible with libertarian freedom because its counterfactual facts fully explain and infallibly determine the relevant agent choices.
The move challenges the internal coherence of Hernandez's account of freedom, a central resource in the theistic explanations presented during the debate.
Hernandez's repeated endorsement of both Molinism and libertarian free will as mutually compatible doctrines.
Schieber begins his substantive closing response by invoking a philosophical incompatibility argument against combining Molinist counterfactuals with libertarian agency.
Appealing to the fall does not explain animal suffering because it either conflicts with prehistoric evidence or fails to predict the specific teleological structure of predation and deprivation.
This move directly contests the proposed theistic explanation for animal suffering, one of the principal comparative issues specified by the motion.
Hernandez's appeal to the human fall as a causal or theological explanation for animal suffering.
Schieber argues that a literal fall conflicts with modern science, while a nonliteral appeal does not predict either the fall itself or the organized forms of animal harm.
The soul-building animal theodicy inherits an unsupported value principle and yields implausible consequences concerning God's character and the dependence of virtues on suffering.
The argument attacks another principal theistic explanation for animal suffering by challenging both its normative foundation and its implications for divine perfection.
Hernandez's soul-building account in which earthly suffering enables virtue and animals later receive compensatory deification.
Schieber reconstructs the proposed soul-building account, then argues that its preference for freely earned virtue lacks adequate support and produces counterintuitive implications.
